safetyNote: Edible only after reliable identification of each specimen. Poisonous Clitocybe rivulosa and related white funnels can grow in the same grassy habitat and can also form rings. A fairy ring or white spore print alone does not establish this species. Do not eat an uncertain collection.

sections.title: Cap and gills
sections.text: Marasmius oreades is a small grassland mushroom with a smooth tan to reddish-buff cap, typically about 2–5 cm across. The cap changes colour as it dries, becoming paler, and often retains a broad low umbo as it flattens. Marginal grooves can be faint rather than prominent. Its white to cream gills are broad and conspicuously spaced; they are narrowly attached or nearly free, never decurrent. The spore print is white.

sections.title: Stem and habitat
sections.text: The slender, pale stem is remarkably tough and pliable for such a small mushroom. It has no ring or volva. The species grows in lawns, meadows and other grassy places, sometimes in arcs or fairy rings. Dried fruit bodies can revive after rain. Ring formation is not unique to this species.

sections.title: Dangerous lookalikes
sections.text: The poisonous fool’s funnel, Clitocybe rivulosa, can occur in the same grass and also has a white spore print. It more often has crowded gills that run down the stem, unlike the distant, non-decurrent gills of M. oreades. Other small brown or pale mushrooms, including poisonous Inocybe species, also require consideration. Check the whole mushroom and every specimen; colour, smell and habitat alone are insufficient.

sections.title: About the plate
sections.text: The plate shows a complete adult, a younger convex specimen, a longitudinal cut and separate cap top and underside views. The broad, distant gills and wiry stem are emphasised. It illustrates a representative appearance, not all moisture-related colour variation.
